title: Pepper-spraying didn't kill man, report says
article: Kasim Cakmak, 37, died May 11 from "excited delirium due to chronic paranoid schizophrenia," says a recent report by chief medical examiner Dr. Graeme Dowling.
Cakmak, a diagnosed schizophrenic on medication, was at the Alberta Mental Health Board's downtown Community Living Program when he flew into a rage.
The Mental Health Crisis Response team was called to take him to Alberta Hospital, but he became more agitated and slapped a nurse.
Two police officers arrived to help with the transfer and Cakmak got more angry.
The officers pepper-sprayed him, handcuffed him on the ground, then noticed he had stopped breathing.

In some rare cases, psychiatric patients and people high on cocaine develop excited delirium. They become quite aggressive and violent, sometimes developing super-human strength, for no apparent reason, Dowling said.
"When people do restrain them, all of a sudden they stop breathing," Dowling said. "It has nothing to do with the restraint."
A Calgary man with schizophrenia died from excited delirium in 1996 after police pepper-sprayed him during an arrest.
Edmonton police earlier ruled no excessive force was used in Cakmak's case.
